name: Ampicillin

fields.mechanism_of_action: Ampicillin is a penicillin-class antibacterial; the ampicillin for injection label describes its antibacterial activity against Gram-positive organisms (haemolytic and non-haemolytic streptococci, Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-penicillinase-producing staphylococci, Clostridium spp., Bacillus anthracis, Listeria monocytogenes and most strains of enterococci) and Gram-negative organisms (Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, Proteus mirabilis and many strains of Salmonella, Shigella and E. coli), and states that AMPICILLIN does not resist destruction by penicillinase (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP (Sagent Pharmaceuticals, revised September 2025), CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY - Microbiology). Class-level mechanism statement, taken from the FDA amoxicillin label because the ampicillin label does not describe the mechanism: amoxicillin 'is similar to penicillin in its bactericidal action against susceptible bacteria during the stage of active multiplication. It acts through the inhibition of cell wall biosynthesis that leads to the death of the bacteria' (FDA label, Amoxicillin tablets, for oral suspension, chewable tablets and capsules, section 12.4 MICROBIOLOGY, Mechanism of Action). Ampicillin diffuses readily into most body tissues and fluids, but penetration into cerebrospinal fluid and brain occurs only when the meninges are inflamed (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY).
indications: Respiratory tract infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (penicillinase and non-penicillinase-producing), Haemophilus influenzae and Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)

Bacterial meningitis caused by E. coli, Group B streptococci and other Gram-negative bacteria (Listeria monocytogenes, N. meningitidis); the addition of an aminoglycoside with ampicillin may increase its effectiveness against Gram-negative bacteria (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)

Septicemia and endocarditis caused by susceptible Gram-positive organisms including Streptococcus spp., penicillin G-susceptible staphylococci and enterococci; Gram-negative sepsis caused by E. coli, Proteus mirabilis and Salmonella spp. responds to ampicillin; endocarditis due to enterococcal strains usually responds to intravenous therapy, and the addition of an aminoglycoside may enhance the effectiveness of ampicillin when treating streptococcal endocarditis (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)
Urinary tract infections caused by sensitive strains of E. coli and Proteus mirabilis (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)

Gastrointestinal infections caused by Salmonella typhi (typhoid fever), other Salmonella spp. and Shigella spp. (dysentery), which usually respond to oral or intravenous therapy (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)

WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 24th list (2025), section 5.1.6.1: ampicillin is first choice for community-acquired pneumonia (severe) and second choice for acute bacterial meningitis, complicated intra-abdominal infections (mild to moderate), complicated severe acute malnutrition and sepsis in neonates and children
Kenya Essential Medicines List 2023, section 7.2.1.4: ampicillin powder for injection, 500 mg vial, Level of Use 4 (primary hospital); classified in the WHO AWaRe 'Access' group (Appendix 7)
contraindications: A history of a previous hypersensitivity reaction to any of the penicillins is a contraindication (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, CONTRAINDICATIONS)
side_effects: Untoward reactions are expected to be essentially limited to sensitivity phenomena and are more likely to occur in individuals who have previously demonstrated hypersensitivity to penicillins and in those with a history of allergy, asthma, hay fever or urticaria (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, ADVERSE REACTIONS)
Gastrointestinal: glossitis, stomatitis, black 'hairy' tongue, nausea, vomiting, enterocolitis, pseudomembranous colitis and diarrhoea (usually associated with oral dosage forms) (ADVERSE REACTIONS)

Hypersensitivity: skin rashes and urticaria reported frequently; a few cases of exfoliative dermatitis and erythema multiforme; linear IgA bullous dermatosis reported; anaphylaxis is the most serious reaction and has usually been associated with the parenteral dosage form (ADVERSE REACTIONS)

Liver: a moderate rise in serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), particularly in infants, with significance unknown; mild transitory SGOT elevations in individuals receiving larger (two to four times) than usual and oft-repeated intramuscular injections, with evidence indicating GOT is released at the site of intramuscular injection and does not necessarily indicate liver involvement (ADVERSE REACTIONS)

Hemic and lymphatic: anaemia, thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilia, leukopenia and agranulocytosis reported during penicillin therapy; usually reversible on discontinuation and believed to be hypersensitivity phenomena (ADVERSE REACTIONS)

dosage.adult: Infections of the respiratory tract and soft tissues: patients weighing 40 kg or more 250 mg to 500 mg every 6 hours. Infections of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts (including those caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae in females): patients weighing 40 kg or more 500 mg every 6 hours. Urethritis in males due to N. gonorrhoeae: two doses of 500 mg each at an interval of 8 to 12 hours, treatment may be repeated if necessary or extended if required. Bacterial meningitis: adults and children 150 to 200 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 3 to 4 hours, treatment may be initiated with intravenous drip therapy and continued with intramuscular injections. Septicemia: adults and children 150 to 200 mg/kg/day, starting with intravenous administration for at least three days and continuing with the intramuscular route every 3 to 4 hours. The doses for the preceding infections may be given by either the intramuscular or intravenous route, and a change to oral ampicillin may be made when appropriate. Treatment of all infections should be continued for a minimum of 48 to 72 hours beyond the time that the patient becomes asymptomatic or evidence of bacterial eradication is obtained; a minimum of 10 days' treatment is recommended for any infection caused by Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci to help prevent acute rheumatic fever or acute glomerulonephritis (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION).
dosage.paediatric: Patients weighing less than 40 kg: respiratory tract and soft tissue infections 25 to 50 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses at 6- to 8-hour intervals; gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract infections 50 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses at 6- to 8-hour intervals. Bacterial meningitis: adults and children 150 to 200 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 3 to 4 hours. Neonates (less than or equal to 28 days of postnatal age) - dosage for bacterial meningitis and septicemia is based on gestational age and postnatal age: gestational age less than or equal to 34 weeks with postnatal age less than or equal to 7 days, 100 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 12 hours; gestational age less than or equal to 34 weeks with postnatal age 8 to less than 28 days or gestational age greater than 34 weeks with postnatal age less than or equal to 28 days, 150 mg/kg/day in equally divided doses every 12 hours or every 8 hours (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION and Table 3). Guidelines for administration to children, including neonates, are given in the DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION section of the label (PRECAUTIONS - Pediatric Use).

interactions: Allopurinol: the concurrent administration of allopurinol and ampicillin increases substantially the incidence of skin rashes in patients receiving both drugs compared with patients receiving ampicillin alone; it is not known whether this potentiation is due to allopurinol or the hyperuricemia present in these patients (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Drug Interactions)

Drug/laboratory test interactions: with high urine concentrations of ampicillin, false-positive glucose reactions may occur if Clinitest, Benedict's solution or Fehling's solution are used; glucose tests based on enzymatic glucose oxidase reactions (such as Clinistix or Tes-Tape) are recommended (PRECAUTIONS - Drug/Laboratory Test Interactions)
fields.monitoring: As with any potent drug, periodic assessment of organ system function, including renal, hepatic and haematopoietic, should be made during prolonged therapy (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Laboratory Tests). Transient elevation of serum transaminase has been observed following administration of ampicillin and its significance is not known (PRECAUTIONS - Laboratory Tests). Bacteriology studies to determine the causative organisms and their susceptibility to ampicillin should be performed, and therapy may be instituted prior to obtaining results of susceptibility testing (INDICATIONS AND USAGE). In chronic urinary tract and intestinal infections, frequent bacteriological and clinical appraisal is necessary (DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION). Monitor for diarrhoea, which may indicate C. difficile-associated diarrhoea, reported over two months after antibacterial use (WARNINGS).
fields.patient_counselling: Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs including ampicillin should only be used to treat bacterial infections and do not treat viral infections such as the common cold; when ampicillin is prescribed to treat a bacterial infection, patients should be told that although it is common to feel better early in the course of therapy, the medication should be taken exactly as directed, because skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may decrease the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood that bacteria will develop resistance and will not be treatable with ampicillin or other antibacterial drugs in the future (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Information for Patients). Diarrhoea is a common problem caused by antibiotics which usually ends when the antibiotic is discontinued; sometimes after starting treatment, patients can develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even as late as two or more months after having taken the last dose of the antibiotic, and if this occurs patients should contact their physician as soon as possible (PRECAUTIONS - Information for Patients).
warnings: Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactoid) reactions have been reported in patients on penicillin therapy; although anaphylaxis is more frequent following parenteral therapy, it has occurred in patients on oral penicillins, and these reactions are more apt to occur in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity and/or a history of sensitivity to multiple allergens; before initiating therapy with a penicillin, careful inquiry should be made concerning previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins and other allergens, and if an allergic reaction occurs the drug should be discontinued and appropriate therapy instituted. SERIOUS ANAPHYLACTOID REACTIONS REQUIRE IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY TREATMENT WITH EPINEPHRINE, OXYGEN, INTRAVENOUS STEROIDS, AND AIRWAY MANAGEMENT, INCLUDING INTUBATION, SHOULD ALSO BE ADMINISTERED AS INDICATED (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, WARNINGS)

Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea (CDAD) has been reported with use of nearly all antibacterial agents including ampicillin for injection and may range from mild diarrhoea to fatal colitis; CDAD must be considered in all patients who present with diarrhoea after antibiotic use, including over two months after the administration of antibacterial agents, and if CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued with appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile and surgical evaluation instituted as clinically indicated (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, WARNINGS)

Skin rash in infectious mononucleosis: a high percentage (43 to 100 percent) of patients with infectious mononucleosis who receive ampicillin develop a skin rash, typically appearing 7 to 10 days after the start of oral ampicillin therapy and lasting a few days to a week after discontinuation; the rash is usually maculopapular, pruritic and generalized, so administration of ampicillin is not recommended in patients with mononucleosis, although it is not known whether these patients are truly allergic to ampicillin (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, PRECAUTIONS - General)

Possible superinfection: the possibility of superinfections with mycotic organisms or bacterial pathogens should be kept in mind during therapy; in such cases discontinue the drug and substitute appropriate treatment (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, PRECAUTIONS - General)

Rapid intravenous administration may result in convulsive seizures: for direct intravenous use, administer slowly over at least 10 to 15 minutes (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, DIRECTIONS FOR USE)
precautions: Reserve the parenteral form for moderately severe and severe infections and for patients who are unable to take the oral forms; a change to oral ampicillin may be made as soon as appropriate (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, INDICATIONS AND USAGE)

Use only freshly prepared solutions: intramuscular and intravenous injections should be administered within one hour after preparation since potency may decrease significantly after this period (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, DIRECTIONS FOR USE)
Bacteriostatic Water for Injection, USP is not to be used as a diluent when the product will be used in newborns (DIRECTIONS FOR USE)

Prescribing ampicillin for injection in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to provide benefit and increases the risk of development of drug-resistant bacteria (PRECAUTIONS - General)
As with any potent drug, periodic assessment of organ system function, including renal, hepatic and haematopoietic, should be made during prolonged therapy (PRECAUTIONS - Laboratory Tests)

Storage: store the dry powder at 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) [USP Controlled Room Temperature]; the product is sterile, nonpyrogenic and preservative-free, and the container closure is not made with natural rubber latex (Ampicillin for Injection, USP label, HOW SUPPLIED - Storage Conditions)
serious_adverse_reactions: Anaphylaxis is the most serious reaction experienced and has usually been associated with the parenteral dosage form; serious anaphylactic reactions require the immediate use of epinephrine, oxygen and intravenous steroids (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, ADVERSE REACTIONS and WARNINGS)
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, ranging from mild diarrhoea to fatal colitis, with pseudomembranous colitis and haemorrhagic colitis reported (WARNINGS and ADVERSE REACTIONS)
Agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and thrombocytopenic purpura (ADVERSE REACTIONS)
Seizures, including with rapid intravenous administration of ampicillin sodium (ADVERSE REACTIONS and DIRECTIONS FOR USE)
Exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme and linear IgA bullous dermatosis (ADVERSE REACTIONS)
fields.pregnancy_category: B (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Pregnancy)
fields.pregnancy_guidance: Pregnancy Category B: reproduction studies have been performed in laboratory animals at doses several times the human dose and have revealed no evidence of adverse effects due to ampicillin. There are, however, no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, this drug should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Pregnancy). Oral ampicillin-class antibiotics are poorly absorbed during labor; studies in guinea pigs showed that intravenous administration of ampicillin slightly decreased uterine tone and frequency of contractions but moderately increased the height and duration of contractions, and it is not known whether use of these drugs in humans during labor or delivery has immediate or delayed adverse effects on the fetus, prolongs the duration of labor, or increases the likelihood that forceps delivery or other obstetrical intervention or resuscitation of the newborn will be necessary (PRECAUTIONS - Labor and Delivery).
fields.lactation_guidance: Ampicillin is excreted in trace amounts in human milk; therefore, caution should be exercised when ampicillin-class antibiotics are administered to a nursing woman (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, PRECAUTIONS - Nursing Mothers).
fields.overdose: In cases of overdose, discontinue medication, treat symptomatically and institute supportive measures as required. In patients with renal function impairment, ampicillin-class antibiotics can be removed by hemodialysis but not by peritoneal dialysis (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, OVERDOSAGE).
fields.pharmacokinetics: Ampicillin for injection diffuses readily into most body tissues and fluids; however, penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid and brain occurs only when the meninges are inflamed. Ampicillin is excreted largely unchanged in the urine and its excretion can be delayed by concurrent administration of probenecid. Due to maturational changes in renal function, the ampicillin half-life decreases as postmenstrual age (gestational age plus postnatal age) increases for infants with a postnatal age of less than 28 days. The active form appears in the bile in higher concentrations than those found in serum. Ampicillin is the least serum-bound of all the penicillins, averaging about 20% compared with approximately 60 to 90% for other penicillins, and ampicillin for injection has been well tolerated by most patients and has been given in doses of 2 grams daily for many weeks without adverse reactions (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY).
clinical_pearls: Ampicillin is not resistant to penicillinase: it is destroyed by penicillinase-producing staphylococci, so antistaphylococcal cover requires another agent (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY - Microbiology)
The ampicillin rash in infectious mononucleosis occurs in 43 to 100% of patients and is not necessarily a true penicillin allergy (PRECAUTIONS - General)
Give the intravenous dose slowly over at least 10 to 15 minutes: more rapid administration may result in convulsive seizures (DIRECTIONS FOR USE)

This monograph covers ampicillin alone. Ampicillin with sulbactam (UNASYN, marketed as a separate injectable combination) is a different medicine with its own label and was not used as a source here, even though the database row previously listed 'Ampicillin and Sulbactam' as a brand for this drug
The label's dosing is expressed per 40 kg body weight, so all paediatric and adult doses below 40 kg are weight-based (DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION)

A pharmacy bulk package presentation of ampicillin for injection also exists on DailyMed (NorthStar Rx, setid 3b683547-48ac-48ca-8fd4-6866fd17be34); it states the same indications, warnings and dosing but is intended for preparing intravenous admixtures only

Both the WHO eEML and KEML place ampicillin in the AWaRe 'Access' group, and KEML 2023 lists it at Level of Use 4 (primary hospital) as a 500 mg powder for injection vial (KEML 2023, section 7.2.1.4 and Appendix 7)
fields.administration_instructions: For intramuscular use, dissolve the contents of the vial with the amount of Sterile Water for Injection, USP or Bacteriostatic Water for Injection, USP listed in the label table (1 g vial in 3.5 mL giving 4 mL at 250 mg/mL; 2 g vial in 6.8 mL giving 8 mL at 250 mg/mL); the 125 mg vial is intended primarily for pediatric use. For direct intravenous use, dissolve 1 g or 2 g in 7.4 mL or 14.8 mL respectively of Sterile Water for Injection, USP or Bacteriostatic Water for Injection, USP and administer slowly over at least 10 to 15 minutes, as more rapid administration may result in convulsive seizures. For administration by intravenous drip, reconstitute as for direct intravenous use and then dilute with intravenous solution; stability studies in 0.9% sodium chloride injection (up to 30 mg/mL, 8 hours at room temperature) and 5% dextrose injection are given in the label. Use only freshly prepared solutions; administer within one hour after preparation; inspect parenteral products visually for particulate matter and discoloration before administration; do not use Bacteriostatic Water for Injection in newborns. Store the dry powder at 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) (FDA label, Ampicillin for Injection, USP, DIRECTIONS FOR USE and HOW SUPPLIED - Storage Conditions).

notes: The table stores this agent as 'Ampicillin' with brand_names ['Ampicillin and Sulbactam']; that brand refers to the UNASYN combination product (ampicillin sodium plus sulbactam sodium), which is a different medicine with its own FDA label, so it has been removed and brand_names is now empty because no ampicillin-only brand product could be verified on DailyMed. The content here is drawn from the FDA label for Ampicillin for Injection, USP (Sagent Pharmaceuticals, revised September 2025), which covers the parenteral presentation only (125 mg, 1 g and 2 g vials); oral ampicillin capsules/tablets are not covered by this label and no oral ampicillin label was used, although the label's indications mention that a change to oral ampicillin may be made as soon as appropriate. A pharmacy bulk package version of the same product (NorthStar Rx) is noted but was not used as the primary source. Since the ampicillin label does not describe the mechanism of action, the mechanism field is explicitly flagged as a class-level statement taken from the FDA amoxicillin label. The WHO eEML and KEML list ampicillin as a powder for injection only, in the AWaRe 'Access' group. FDA pregnancy categories are obsolete under the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule and are reported only because this label still states Category B.
